title: Tissue Fixation, Processing, Embedding & H&E Staining

references.label: Standard histotechnology laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To convert fresh tissue into a thin, stained, permanent slide suitable for microscopic examination, preserving cellular and tissue architecture through a multi-stage process.
principle: Fresh tissue autolyzes and putrefies rapidly, so it must first be chemically fixed (commonly in formalin, which cross-links proteins and halts enzymatic degradation) to preserve structure. Fixed tissue is then processed — dehydrated through graded alcohols, cleared (alcohol replaced with a clearing agent miscible with paraffin), and infiltrated with molten paraffin wax — so it becomes firm enough to section at a few micrometers thickness on a microtome. Sections are mounted on slides, and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is applied: hematoxylin (a basic dye) stains acidic/basophilic structures (chiefly nuclei) blue-purple, while eosin (an acidic dye) stains basic/eosinophilic structures (chiefly cytoplasm and extracellular matrix) pink, giving the classic contrast pathologists use to assess tissue architecture and cellular detail.
requiredMaterials: Microtome and water bath for section flotation
requiredReagents: Clearing agent (e.g. xylene or a validated substitute)

procedure.note: Under-fixation and delayed fixation are common, hard-to-reverse sources of poor downstream staining and morphology.
procedure.instruction: Fix fresh tissue promptly in an adequate volume of fixative relative to tissue size, for the time specified by the fixative and tissue thickness in use.
Process the fixed tissue through graded dehydration, clearing, and paraffin infiltration steps, following the processor's validated schedule for the tissue type/thickness.
Embed the processed tissue in a paraffin block, orienting it appropriately for the plane of section needed.
Section the block on a microtome at the specified thickness (commonly a few micrometers for routine H&E), float the ribbon on a warm water bath to remove wrinkles, and mount onto a charged slide.

procedure.note: Exact staining timing is method- and reagent-batch-dependent and should follow the laboratory's validated, periodically-verified protocol rather than a fixed universal time.
procedure.instruction: Deparaffinize and rehydrate the section, then stain with hematoxylin, differentiate/blue, counterstain with eosin, dehydrate, clear, and coverslip with mounting medium.
Examine the finished slide under the microscope to confirm section quality (no major folds/tears, adequate staining contrast) before it proceeds to pathologist review.

observations: A well-processed H&E section shows crisp blue-purple nuclear detail against pink cytoplasmic/stromal background, with intact tissue architecture free of major processing artifacts.
interpretation: H&E is the foundational stain pathologists use to assess tissue architecture and cellular morphology; specific diagnoses often require additional special stains or immunohistochemistry beyond this foundational entry's scope.
criticalNotes: Fixation quality and timing cannot be fully corrected later in processing — inadequate initial fixation compromises everything downstream.
precautions: Formalin and xylene (or clearing-agent alternatives) are hazardous chemicals requiring proper ventilation, PPE, and disposal per chemical safety protocol.
Track tissue/block/slide identification meticulously through every step — a mix-up in histopathology has severe patient-safety consequences.
limitations: Processing schedules are tissue-type and thickness dependent; a schedule validated for standard-sized tissue is not automatically appropriate for very large or very small/fragile specimens.
biosafetyNotes: Treat all tissue as potentially infectious; handle fixative and clearing-agent chemical hazards per the facility's chemical hygiene plan in addition to standard biological precautions.
